query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating enhanced free energy sampling techniques (e.g., metadynamics or umbrella sampling) with machine-learned interatomic potentials calibrated on representative high-entropy alloy systems enables accurate and efficient prediction of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-component high-entropy alloys in their high-temperature solid state approaching melting.
generation.intervention: Apply an integrated free energy sampling protocol using enhanced sampling techniques combined with ML-calibrated interatomic potentials.
generation.conditions: High-temperature regimes near the melting transition for a representative set of HEA compositions under controlled simulation integration paths.
generation.structural_mediator: The free energy landscape governing the solid-to-liquid phase transformation.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced sampling methods overcome the sampling barriers associated with complex multi-element interactions, while the ML potentials ensure computational efficiency and capture the intricate energetics of melting, yielding fusion properties that align with experimental calorimetric measurements.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will predict melting temperatures and fusion properties with deviations within an acceptable error margin (tentatively below 10% relative error) compared to high-temperature experimental measurements.
generation.baseline: Traditional approaches such as differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), high-temperature calorimetry, and standard computational methods (ab initio and CALPHAD) that individually lack either the broad applicability or the efficiency required for HEAs.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to perform well within the calibrated compositional space of HEAs; however, it may be less applicable to alloys with extreme elemental imbalances or unforeseen complex phase transitions beyond the calibration range.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the full transferability of ML potentials across all HEA compositions and the sensitivity of the enhanced sampling parameters (e.g., window selection and integration path) in accurately resolving the free energy barriers.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a series of well-characterized high-entropy alloy compositions and perform high-temperature calorimetry experiments to directly measure their melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase properties. Independently simulate these properties using the integrated free energy sampling approach under identical composition and temperature conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across multiple HEA compositions, the experimental fusion properties differ by more than 10% relative to the predictions from the integrated free energy sampling approach, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems. The LSF methodology proposed by Dong et al . [29] , [30] was adopted to describe the finite-temperature magnetic state of each alloy species in PM CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The root-mean-square magnetic moment m I ( w , T ) [30] , which is formulated as m I = ∫ μ 2 ⋅ x ( μ ) d μ with x ( μ ) being the spin-density distribution of longitudinal magnetic component μ , was used to represent the LSF energetics at thermal excitations in both the fcc and hcp phases. For the sake of computational feasibility of determining { m I }, we used the ‘fluctuating medium approximation’ and the ‘one shot from static equilibrium approach’ [29] . The present LSF methodology has been applied to PM bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, and the predicted finite-temperature properties such as single-crystal elastic constants [29] , [30] , lattice expansion [34] and intrinsic energy barriers [39] confirm the accurate description of the magnetic state at elevated temperatures.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

decision.trend: Early work in high‐entropy alloys focused on measuring high-temperature mechanical and microstructural properties using traditional experimental methods (e.g., DSC and calorimetry) and limited computational techniques such as ab initio and CALPHAD models. Over time, studies (as seen in PMC6908586, PMC11206460, and PMC10213035) began exploring high-temperature phase stability and complex structural transformations, hinting at the limitations of conventional approaches when applied to multi‐component systems. Although these works improved understanding of high‐temperature behaviors and phase transitions, they did not provide a unified, efficient, and accurate method to obtain fusion properties across the entire HEA compositional space.
decision.unsolved: A robust technique to determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the diverse high-entropy-alloy family is still missing. Existing experimental and computational methods either suffer from efficiency or accuracy issues when applied to multi-principal element systems, leaving the complex multi-element interactions and the broad compositional range inadequately sampled and validated.
decision.lever: integrated free energy sampling using enhanced sampling techniques (such as metadynamics or umbrella sampling) combined with machine-learned interatomic potentials calibrated on representative HEA systems
decision.why: This approach logically follows the trend toward blending computational efficiency with physical fidelity. It builds upon earlier high-temperature and phase-stability studies by explicitly mapping the free energy landscape associated with melting transitions in multi-component alloys. By enabling systematic determination of fusion properties with controlled key parameters (e.g. sampling temperature windows and integration paths) and offering an experimentally verifiable output (via dedicated high-temperature calorimetry), it directly targets the identified gap.
